set.note: The phrase was made famous by the psychologist William James in 1890 to describe how thought flows.
set.why: It is a key feature of modern novels such as James Joyce's Ulysses and Virginia Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway.

why: Note falsely says William James first used the phrase (Alexander Bain used it in 1855; James popularized it in 1890). 'Interior monologue' is a related but distinct technique, not a synonym. US title style 'Mrs. Dalloway'.

set.note: Sometimes called "blood poisoning," but doctors say that older name is not accurate.

why: Sepsis Alliance: 'blood poisoning' is an older, inaccurate term and should not be used interchangeably with sepsis, so it cannot be the tested synonym; note claimed it is simply the everyday name.

set.why: Named and made famous by John Rawls in his 1971 book A Theory of Justice, it is a widely used way to think about what makes a society fair.

why: 'Proposed by John Rawls in 1971' is inaccurate: the thought experiment was described earlier by Vickrey (1945) and Harsanyi (1953); Rawls coined the term and made it famous.

set.def: a planet outside our solar system, usually one that circles a star other than our Sun
set.why: Thousands have been found, and scientists study them to learn how planets form and whether life could exist elsewhere.

why: NASA defines an exoplanet as any planet beyond our solar system, including rogue planets bound to no star; 'why' claim that they are 'the main places' searched for life is unsupported (Mars, Europa, Enceladus are major targets).

set.def: a link between two atoms that holds them together because they share one or more pairs of electrons

why: Double and triple covalent bonds share two or three pairs; 'a pair' is inaccurate.

set.def: a straight line that a curve on a graph gets closer and closer to as it stretches farther out

why: Curves can touch or cross an asymptote (e.g., sin x / x crosses y = 0 repeatedly), so 'without ever quite touching' is false as a definition.

set.def: the sorting of sick or injured people by how urgently they need care, so the most urgent cases are treated first

why: 'Worst cases are treated first' is misleading: in disasters the most badly hurt who are unlikely to survive may be given lower priority; triage ranks by urgency.

'Comfort care' usually means end-of-life care focused only on comfort after curative treatment stops, which contradicts this item's own point that palliative care can accompany cure-directed treatment; not a true synonym.

set.def: a realistic fake video, photo or voice clip, made with AI, of a real person doing or saying something they never did

why: Def mentions voice clips but only 'doing'; deepfakes most often fake speech (as in the item's own example and cloze).

set.def: a drawing method that makes a flat picture look deep by making parallel lines seem to meet at one far point
set.why: Developed in Florence in the early 1400s, it changed Western painting and is still widely taught in drawing classes.

why: Parallel lines only appear to meet; 'in every drawing class' is an unverifiable overclaim.

ex: When Fatima's lips swelled after eating a cookie with nuts, her friend used her epinephrine pen to treat the anaphylaxis.
A bee sting can trigger anaphylaxis in people who are badly allergic to the venom.

why: Epinephrine treats anaphylaxis but does not reliably 'stop' it (the item's own note says an ER visit is still needed).
Cloze 'it would break the law of ___' about perpetual motion: 'entropy' (the second law of thermodynamics) also forbids perpetual motion and fits sensibly.
(f) 'opposite of martial law': 'rule of law' reads as a near-opposite of military rule, competing with 'civilian rule'.
